claim: Rice yield was significantly higher in the RA treatment than in the RM treatment in the rice-carp experiment (F1,10=7.828, p = 0.019).
source: We found that rice yield was significantly higher in the RA treatment (the treatment with the coculture of rice and an aquatic animal) than in the RM treatment (the treatment with rice monoculture) in the rice-carp experiment (F1,10=7.828, p = 0.019)
evidence: Statistical test results (F-statistic and p-value) from field experiments comparing rice yields between treatments.

claim: Rice yield was significantly higher in the RA treatment than in the RM treatment in the rice-crab experiment (F1,10=5.957, p = 0.035).
source: We found that rice yield was significantly higher in the RA treatment (the treatment with the coculture of rice and an aquatic animal) than in the RM treatment (the treatment with rice monoculture) in the rice-carp experiment (F1,10=7.828, p = 0.019), the rice-crab experiment (F1,10=5.957, p = 0.035)
evidence: Statistical test results from field experiments comparing rice yields between treatments.

claim: Rice yield was significantly higher in the RA treatment than in the RM treatment in the rice-turtle experiment (F1,10=12.472, p = 0.005).

claim: Average rice yield over 4 years in the RA treatment was 9.13% ± 3.11% higher for rice-carp compared to rice monoculture.

claim: Average rice yield over 4 years in the RA treatment was 12.05% ± 1.16% higher for rice-crabs compared to rice monoculture.

evidence: Calculated percentage increase from 4-year field experiment data.

claim: Average rice yield over 4 years in the RA treatment was 8.69% ± 1.74% higher for rice-turtles compared to rice monoculture.

evidence: Calculated percentage increase from 4-year field experiment data.

claim: The average annual aquatic animal yield was 0.85 t ha–1 for rice-carp systems.

claim: The average annual aquatic animal yield was 0.56 t ha–1 for rice-crab systems.

claim: Increases in species number can increase ecosystem productivity and stability in natural ecosystems.
source: In natural ecosystems, experiments have shown that increases in species number can increase ecosystem productivity and stability (Hector et al., 1999; Tilman et al., 2006; Loreau and de Mazancourt, 2013; Tilman et al., 2014; van der Plas, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Positive effects of species diversity on ecosystem functioning are mainly explained by niche partitioning, facilitation, and complementary resource use.
source: These positive effects of species diversity on ecosystem functioning are mainly explained by niche partitioning, facilitation, and complementary resource use (Cardinale et al., 2002; Isbell et al., 2009; Cardinale, 2011; Brooker et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Interspecific facilitation or complementary resource use are common in terrestrial, marine, and wetland ecosystems.
source: Interspecific facilitation (which occurs when one species makes conditions more favorable for another species) or complementary resource use are common in terrestrial, marine, and wetland ecosystems (Bruno et al., 2003; Brooker et al., 2007; He et al., 2013; Bulleri et al., 2015; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Rice-aquatic animal coculture systems can increase rice yields and soil fertility while reducing the need for fertilizers and pesticides compared to rice monoculture.
source: Field surveys and experiments have shown that these coculture systems can increase rice yields and soil fertility while reducing the need for fertilizers and pesticides compared to rice monoculture (Xie et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Animal behaviors are important drivers of ecosystem processes such as carbon and nutrient cycling, and energy flux.
source: Animal behaviors (e.g. moving and grazing) are important drivers of ecosystem processes (e.g. carbon and nutrient cycling, and energy flux) (Vanni et al., 2006; Schmitz et al., 2018; McInturf et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Grazing, 'muddying', and burrowing by aquatic animals have important roles in nutrient cycling in wetland or aquatic ecosystems.
source: In wetland or aquatic ecosystems, grazing, 'muddying', and burrowing by aquatic animals have important roles in nutrient cycling (Vanni, 2002; Thrush et al., 2006; Devlin et al., 2015; Atkinson et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Carp and crabs can greatly reduce weeds in rice-carp systems.
source: Carp and crabs, for example, can greatly reduce weeds in rice-carp systems (Frei and Becker, 2005b; Xie et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Carp and crabs can greatly reduce weeds in rice-crab systems.
source: Carp and crabs, for example, can greatly reduce weeds in rice-carp systems (Frei and Becker, 2005b; Xie et al., 2011) and in rice-crab systems (Lv et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Grazers can accelerate nutrient cycling in natural grassland and freshwater ecosystems by increasing nutrient availability in soil and nutrient-use efficiency of plants.
source: Many studies have shown that grazers can accelerate nutrient cycling in natural grassland and freshwater ecosystems by increasing nutrient availability in soil and nutrient-use efficiency of plants (McNaughton et al., 1997; Atkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ammonia represents from 75% to 85% of the N in aquatic animal excretions.
source: Because ammonia represents from 75% to 85% of the N in aquatic animal excretions (Chakraborty and Chakraborty, 1998), the excretions can be directly utilized by rice plants.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Rice paddies provide food for half of the world's population.
source: Rice paddies provide food for half of the world's population (Gross and Zhao, 2014; Edzesi et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Rice paddies provide ecosystem services including groundwater recharge, flood control, water purification, and the conservation of biodiversity, landscapes, and human cultures.
source: Rice paddies provide food for half of the world's population (Gross and Zhao, 2014; Edzesi et al., 2016), and also provide other ecosystem services, including groundwater recharge, flood control, water purification, and the conservation of biodiversity, landscapes, and human cultures (Bouman et al., 2007; Natuhara, 2013; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The coculture of rice with aquatic animals has been practiced in many countries including Bangladesh, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam.
source: Because paddy fields provide a shallow water habitat suitable for some aquatic animals (e.g. carp, crabs, and softshell turtles), the coculturing of rice with aquatic animals has been practiced in many countries (e.g. Bangladesh, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam) (Halwart and Gupta, 2004; Frei and Becker, 2005b; Ahmed and Garnett, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The common carp (Cyprinus carpio) has adapted to paddy habitats and is predominantly used for rice-carp coculture.
source: The common carp (Cyprinus carpio) has adapted to paddy habitats and is predominantly used for rice-carp coculture (Figure 7A, Xie et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Rice-aquatic animal coculture increases food production by producing both rice grain and aquatic animals.
source: In our field experiment, an average annual aquatic animal yield ranging from 0.52 to 2.57 t ha–1 was produced from the rice fields (Figure 1), suggesting that local farmers can obtain more income from their paddy fields.
evidence: Inferred from the combined production of rice and aquatic animals shown in Figure 1.

claim: Aquatic animals reduce competitors of rice plants by consuming weeds, algae, and phytoplankton.
source: Our dietary reconstruction based on stable-isotope data of δ13C and δ15N showed that carp and crabs obtained 34.8–50.2% of their total food from the rice field, including weeds, macro-algae, and phytoplankton (Figure 3); these results provide indirect evidence that carp and crabs reduced competitors of rice.
evidence: Inferred from dietary reconstruction data showing consumption of rice competitors shown in Figure 3.

claim: Aquatic animal excretions can be directly utilized by rice plants because they contain high levels of ammonia.
source: Because ammonia represents from 75% to 85% of the N in aquatic animal excretions (Chakraborty and Chakraborty, 1998), the excretions can be directly utilized by rice plants.
evidence: Inferred from the high ammonia content in excretions and the fact that ammonia is a plant-available form of nitrogen.

claim: Aquatic animal feces may release nutrients once they are decomposed, or they may be stored in the form of soil organic matter.
source: The aquatic animal feces may release nutrients once they are decomposed, or they may be stored in the form of soil organic matter.
evidence: Statement about potential fates of feces based on general understanding of decomposition processes.

claim: The promotion of N cycling by aquatic animals explains why N-use efficiency of rice was higher and soil N content was more stable in rice-aquatic animal coculture plots than in monoculture plots.
source: Thus, the promotion of N cycling by aquatic animals apparently explains, at least in part, why N-use efficiency of rice was higher and soil N content was more stable in the rice-aquatic animal coculture plots than in the monoculture plots (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observed effects on N-use efficiency and soil N content shown in Figure 1, combined with evidence of N cycling.

claim: Aquatic animals increase nutrient availability for rice plants by enhancing organic matter decomposition.
source: In addition to reducing competition and increasing nutrient availability for rice plants via grazing, aquatic animals apparently increased nutrient availability for rice plants by enhancing organic matter decomposition.
evidence: Inferred from the observed increase in decomposition rates in RA treatments.

claim: Nutrients in organic matter may be released by decomposition and then used by rice plants or other organisms in the field.
source: Nutrients (e.g. N and P) in the organic matter (e.g. unconsumed feed, aquatic animal feces, and leaf litter) may be released by decomposition and then used by rice plants or other organisms in the field.
evidence: Statement based on general understanding of decomposition and nutrient cycling.

claim: Unconsumed or unassimilated feed can function as a fertilizer for rice and can thereby increase rice yield and N content in the soil.
source: These results suggest that N use by cocultured rice and animals can be complementary and can increase N-use efficiency. The results also suggest that the unconsumed or unassimilated feed can function as a fertilizer for rice and can thereby increase the rice yield and the N content in the soil.
evidence: Inferred from 15N tracing data showing feed-N uptake by rice and accumulation in soil.

claim: N use by cocultured rice and animals can be complementary and can increase N-use efficiency.
source: These results suggest that N use by cocultured rice and animals can be complementary and can increase N-use efficiency.
evidence: Inferred from 15N tracing data showing both rice and animals using feed-N.

claim: The P input via feed may contribute to the rice yield increase and the maintenance of soil P in the coculture systems.
source: In our 4-year field experiments, the level of soil total P was similar at the end vs. the beginning under both rice monocultures and rice-animal cocultures (Appendix 1—figure 3), but rice yields were higher and more P was removed with the harvested products with coculture than with monoculture (Appendix 2—table 2). It follows that the P input via feed may contribute to the rice yield increase and the maintenance of soil P in the coculture systems.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that soil P remained stable despite higher P removal in coculture systems, shown in Appendix 1—figure 3 and Appendix 2—table 2.

claim: Rice plants and the three aquatic animals (carp, crabs, and turtles) have similar growing periods and similar water and temperature requirements.
source: In our study, the rice plants and the three aquatic animals (i.e. carp, crabs, and turtles) have a similar growing period and have similar water and temperature requirements, making it possible to develop a rice–aquatic animal partnership.
evidence: Statement based on the experimental design and known biology of the species.

claim: Carp, crabs, and turtles play similar roles in increasing rice yield and N-use efficiency, and in stabilizing soil N despite differing in biological traits and feeding activities.
source: Although carp, crabs, and turtles differ in biological traits and feeding activities, they play similar roles in increasing rice yield and N-use efficiency, and in stabilizing soil N.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental results from all three coculture systems.

claim: Rice-aquatic animal cocultures could produce more food (rice grain and fish) with less fertilizer and pesticides than rice monocultures.
source: Our study suggests that this challenge can be at least partially met by adding certain species of aquatic animals to rice monocultures. The resulting cocultures could produce more food (rice grain and fish) with less fertilizer and pesticides than rice monocultures.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing higher yields, reduced weed biomass (implying less herbicide need), and maintained soil fertility.

claim: Prices for grain and aquatic animal products from rice-aquatic animal cocultures were higher than from local rice monoculture.
source: Moreover, the prices for grain and aquatic animal products from these cocultures were higher than from the local rice monoculture (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Net income was higher for rice-aquatic animal cocultures than for monocultures despite higher costs.
source: Although costs of the cocultures are higher than the costs of monoculture because of the feed input and increased labor required for the management of two species, net income was still higher for cocultures than for monocultures because of the higher prices of the products and the reduced use of fertilizers and pesticides (Hu et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased income has greatly increased farmer enthusiasm for rice–aquatic animal cocultures in China over the last two decades.
source: Over the last two decades in China, the increased income has greatly increased farmer enthusiasm for the rice–aquatic animal cocultures (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Rice-aquatic animal coculture would not cause serious N eutrophication when target aquatic animal yields are below certain thresholds: 2.11 ± 0.22 t ha–1 for rice-carp, 0.66 ± 0.08 t ha–1 for rice-crab, and 3.62 ± 0.25 t ha–1 for rice-turtle.
source: Previous studies, however, found that rice-aquatic animal coculture would not cause serious N eutrophication in the field when the target aquatic animal yields were set below the following thresholds: 2.11 ± 0.22 t ha–1 for rice-carp, 0.66 ± 0.08 t ha–1 for rice-crab, and 3.62 ± 0.25 t ha–1 for rice-turtle coculture systems (Hu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effects of rice-aquatic animal coculture on carbon emission (e.g. CH4 emission) varied among reports.
source: The effects of rice-aquatic animal coculture on carbon emission (e.g. CH4 emission) varied among reports (Ding et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some experiments indicated that CH4 emissions were lower in rice–aquatic animal coculture systems than in rice monocultures.
source: Some experiments indicated that CH4 emissions were lower in rice–aquatic animal coculture systems than in rice monocultures (Yuan et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some experiments indicated that CH4 emissions were higher in rice–aquatic animal coculture systems than in rice monocultures.
source: while other experiments indicated that CH4 emissions were higher in rice–aquatic animal coculture systems than in rice monocultures (Frei and Becker, 2005a; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Differences in CH4 emission could be caused by differences in aquatic animals, natural environments, and field management.
source: These differences in CH4 emission could be caused by differences in aquatic animals, natural environments, and field management (Ding et al., 2020; Dai et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The aquatic animals increased organic matter decomposition in the paddy field, suggesting that the release of nutrients but also of CO2 would be higher with coculture than with monoculture.
source: In our study, the aquatic animals increased organic matter decomposition in the paddy field (Figure 4), suggesting that the release of nutrients but also of CO2 would be higher with coculture than with monoculture.
evidence: Inferred from the observed increase in decomposition rates shown in Figure 4, combined with knowledge that decomposition releases both nutrients and CO2.

claim: Financial returns were higher for rice-turtle systems than for rice-carp and rice-crab systems.
source: In our previous survey, the three typical types of coculture (i.e. rice-carp, rice-crab, and rice-turtle) were compared in terms of financial returns for the farmers. Financial returns were higher for rice-turtle systems (which is the most common type of coculture in south China) than for rice-carp and rice-crab systems (Hu et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Other types of rice-aquatic animal coculture (e.g. rice-prawn/crayfish, rice-frogs, and rice-ducks) are also practiced in China and in other Asian countries.
source: In addition to these three types of coculture, other types (e.g. rice-prawn/crayfish, rice-frogs, and rice-ducks) are also practiced in China and in other Asian countries (Hu et al., 2015; Ahmed and Turchini, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The main components of the feed used in rice-aquatic animal coculture are residues of soybean after the oil has been extracted.
source: In some areas, farmers apply feed to obtain higher animal yield from the cocultures, and the main components of the feed are residues of soybean after the oil has been extracted.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of feed composition in these systems.

claim: The cropland available for soybean production and the integration of rice-aquatic animal coculture with soybean production should be taken into account before substantial increases in coculture area are promoted.
source: Given the millions of hectares of rice fields with suitable conditions for rice-aquatic animal coculture, the cropland available for soybean production and the integration of rice-aquatic animal coculture with soybean production should be taken into account before substantial increases in coculture area are promoted.
evidence: Recommendation based on the need for soybean-based feed and land use considerations.

claim: No herbicides were used in the field experiments.
source: No herbicides were used in the experiment. Values are means ± SE (n = 6).
evidence: Statement in Figure 2 caption describing experimental conditions.

claim: No chemicals were used to control weeds, pests, or diseases during the field experiments.
source: No chemicals were used to control weeds, pests, or diseases during the experiments.
evidence: Statement describing experimental methods.

claim: Three separate field experiments and three separate mesocosm experiments were conducted.
source: Three separate field experiments and three separate mesocosm experiments were conducted.
evidence: Statement describing the experimental design.

claim: Each experiment included a rice monoculture (RM) treatment and a rice-aquatic animal (RA) coculture treatment.
source: Each experiment included a rice monoculture (RM) treatment and a rice-aquatic animal (RA) coculture treatment; RA included feed addition for aquatic animals.
evidence: Statement describing the experimental design.

claim: RA treatment included feed addition for aquatic animals.
source: Each experiment included a rice monoculture (RM) treatment and a rice-aquatic animal (RA) coculture treatment; RA included feed addition for aquatic animals.
evidence: Statement describing the experimental design.

claim: The average annual aquatic animal yield ranged from 0.52 to 2.57 t ha-1 across the three coculture systems.
source: In the field experiments, rice yield was higher with RA than with RM, and RA also produced aquatic animal yields that averaged 0.52–2.57 t ha-1.
evidence: Summary of measured yield data from field experiments.

claim: Compared to their corresponding RMs, the three RAs had significantly higher apparent nitrogen (N)-use efficiency.
source: Compared to their corresponding RMs, the three RAs had significantly higher apparent nitrogen (N)-use efficiency and lower weed infestation, while soil N contents were stable over time.
evidence: Summary of experimental results.

claim: Compared to their corresponding RMs, the three RAs had lower weed infestation.
source: Compared to their corresponding RMs, the three RAs had significantly higher apparent nitrogen (N)-use efficiency and lower weed infestation, while soil N contents were stable over time.
evidence: Summary of experimental results.

claim: Soil N contents were stable over time in the RA treatments.
source: Compared to their corresponding RMs, the three RAs had significantly higher apparent nitrogen (N)-use efficiency and lower weed infestation, while soil N contents were stable over time.
evidence: Summary of experimental results.

claim: 16.0–50.2% of aquatic animal foods were from naturally occurring organisms in the rice fields.
source: Dietary reconstruction analysis based on 13C and 15N showed that 16.0–50.2% of aquatic animal foods were from naturally occurring organisms in the rice fields.
evidence: Results from stable isotope dietary reconstruction analysis.

claim: The organic matter decomposition rate was greater with RA than with RM in the field experiments.
source: Stable-isotope-labeling (13C) in the field experiments indicated that the organic matter decomposition rate was greater with RA than with RM.
evidence: Results from 13C labeling experiment.

claim: Rice used 13.0–35.1% of the aquatic animal feed-N in the mesocosm experiments.
source: Isotope 15N labeling in the mesocosm experiments indicated that rice used 13.0–35.1% of the aquatic animal feed-N.
evidence: Results from 15N labeling experiment in mesocosms.

claim: Rice-aquatic animal coculture increases food production, increases N-use efficiency, and maintains soil N content by reducing weeds and promoting decomposition and complementary N use.
source: All these results suggest that rice-aquatic animal coculture increases food production, increases N-use efficiency, and maintains soil N content by reducing weeds and promoting decomposition and complementary N use.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental results.

claim: Adding species to monocultures may enhance agroecosystem functions.
source: Our study supports the view that adding species to monocultures may enhance agroecosystem functions.
evidence: General conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: Biological simplification and reliance on chemicals have increased concern with low levels of biodiversity in modern, intensive agriculture.
source: Biological simplification and reliance on chemicals have increased the concern with the low levels of biodiversity in modern, intensive agriculture (Li et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2008; Kremen et al., 2012; Ren et al., 2014; Brooker et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Paddy fields provide a shallow water habitat suitable for some aquatic animals (e.g. carp, crabs, and softshell turtles).
source: Because paddy fields provide a shallow water habitat suitable for some aquatic animals (e.g. carp, crabs, and softshell turtles)
evidence: Statement based on known characteristics of paddy fields and aquatic animals.

claim: Feed is often applied in the form of pellets to increase the growth of aquatic animals in coculture systems.
source: Feed is often applied in the form of pellets to increase the growth of aquatic animals in coculture systems (Hu et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significant percentages of the N in the feed is often unconsumed and unassimilated by the animals.
source: Feed is often applied in the form of pellets to increase the growth of aquatic animals in coculture systems (Hu et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2020), and significant percentages of the N in the feed is often unconsumed and unassimilated by the animals.
evidence: Statement based on general knowledge of animal feeding efficiency and supported by citations.

claim: Unconsumed and unassimilated feed-N could be used by rice plants, resulting in higher N-use efficiency and a more stable soil N content in a coculture system than in a rice monoculture.
source: We therefore expected that this unconsumed and unassimilated feed-N could be used by rice plants, resulting in higher N-use efficiency and a more stable soil N content in a coculture system than in a rice monoculture.
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the introduction, later supported by experimental data.

claim: Coculture with aquatic animals would increase rice yield by reducing competitors of rice.
source: Because some fresh water animals (e.g. carp, crabs, crayfish, and softshell turtles) that are cultured in fish ponds or in paddy fields are omnivores and may use weeds, algae, and phytoplankton as food, we expected that the coculture of these aquatic animals would increase rice yield by reducing competitors of rice.
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the introduction, later supported by experimental data.

claim: Cocultured aquatic animals would promote organic matter decomposition because of their feeding activity and would thereby promote nutrient recycling in the paddy ecosystem.
source: We also expected that the cocultured aquatic animals would promote organic matter decomposition because of their feeding activity and would thereby promote nutrient recycling in the paddy ecosystem.
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the introduction, later supported by experimental data.
